title: Communicate with Confidence: A Blueprint for Mastering Every Conversation
guest: Lorraine K. Lee (executive presence and workplace visibility expert, LinkedIn Top Voice, author of Unforgettable Presence) and Leah Wyar (President of Entertainment, Beauty and Style at People Inc / Dotdash Meredith)
summary: A two-part career-reset compilation built on the 'invisible game of power at work': competence becomes credibility, credibility becomes influence, and influence becomes success and compensation. Part 1 with Lorraine K. Lee covers the perception layer (first impressions, video presence, self-advocacy scripts, minimizing language, promotion strategy); Part 2 with Leah Wyar covers the influence layer (work wives, saying yes, navigating politics, taking emotion out of feedback, and balancing career with motherhood).

ideas.idea: Doing the hard work does not get you promoted; being seen does, because talent only pays off when it converts into credibility, influence and revenue.
ideas.detail: The hosts frame the 'invisible game' as competence becoming credibility, credibility becoming influence, and influence becoming success and compensation. January is when scope gets assigned and promotions are decided earlier than most people think.

ideas.idea: First impressions form in as little as a tenth of a second, and most people get them wrong by ignoring nonverbal signals.
ideas.detail: Posture, eye contact, a solid handshake, and not being on your phone matter; being on your cell phone when the interviewer walks out, or sending 'one quick message' at the start of a video call, signals distraction before you have said a word.

ideas.idea: 'Resting business face' on video calls is a silent career killer; the fix is to smile, nod slowly, raise your eyebrows and consciously show engagement.
ideas.detail: At home we relax into neutral or angry-looking expressions, which video magnifies. With limited touch points in a remote day, video presence has to do the work; the hosts note this is especially penalized in women, who are expected to project warmth.

ideas.idea: Hard work does not speak for itself; you must be vocal about your work, and using collaborative 'we/us/our' language makes you seem more senior than 'I' statements.
ideas.detail: Lorraine cites Harvard Business Review data showing collaborative language reads as more senior and impressive, while heavy 'I' statements read as junior. Frame wins as team learnings, ground them in data, and tie them to the company's bottom line.

ideas.idea: Find where the decision makers are actually looking and repeat your wins there, because people need to hear things seven times in seven different ways to retain them.
ideas.detail: At Prezi, with no wins listserv, Lorraine used the company intranet; she also suggests the Slack channel the CEO or target leader reads. A 10am Slack misses APAC and Europe, so post in Slack, then email, then mention it in the team meeting.

ideas.idea: LinkedIn posts should draw on three content pillars, personal, professional and educational, plus a bonus promotional pillar, and nothing on LinkedIn needs to be original.
ideas.detail: Educational is the easiest starting point, professional covers industry news, and personal stories are hardest but resonate most. People connect with the person and the packaging, not the novelty of the content, so stop waiting for a perfectly original thought.

ideas.idea: Adding the word 'because' to a request raises compliance by up to 93 percent, even when the reason is weak.
ideas.detail: Lorraine uses it for deadlines ('fill this out by Friday because I'm excited to share it with the company'). The hosts recall the Xerox copier study where 'because I need to make copies' still got most people to let the requester cut the line, and a friend's mother who gets designer-store discounts just by asking with a 'because'.

ideas.idea: Write 'email haikus': messages short enough to fit on a smartphone screen without scrolling, with subject lines that carry the action.
ideas.detail: The idea comes from Kim Scott, author of Radical Candor. Spending 20-30 minutes to trim saves back-and-forth clarification. Cherie learned similar email hygiene in Glenn Kramon's 'Winning Writing' class at Stanford; Jean notes finance teams write the whole message in the subject line and end it with 'EOM'.

ideas.idea: Using your hands on camera makes you appear warmer, more energetic and more trustworthy, and gestures increase recall of what you say by 33 percent.
ideas.detail: Frame yourself with three to five fingers of space above your head and show some torso so your hands appear naturally; most people keep hands in their lap so viewers only see shoulder twitches. Cherie's Stanford executive presence class taught matching gestures to enumerated points so vocal and visual align.

ideas.idea: Cut minimizing language like 'does that make sense?', 'sorry I'm late' and 'I think', replacing them with 'let me know if you have any questions', 'thank you for your patience' and 'I recommend' or 'the data suggests'.
ideas.detail: 'Does that make sense?' implies you are unsure of what you just said; the replacement keeps collaboration while signaling confidence. Arriving with 'thank you for your patience' starts the meeting on positive footing instead of forcing the other person to reassure you.

ideas.idea: Promotions are decided by a room of people months in advance, so tell your manager you want one at least six months early and repeat it.
ideas.detail: Lorraine initially assumed her manager alone decided and that ambition was obvious; many people do not actually want promotion, so you must say so. Find out who is in the room, what skills are missing, and give yourself time to address gaps. Cherie, as a former manager, describes the legwork of pre-empting objections from other voters.

ideas.idea: Your boss does not have to like your personality to promote you, but they must like what you bring and you must make their life ten times easier.
ideas.detail: Because a manager does so much behind-the-scenes advocacy for a promotion, they need to be invested; that comes from respect for your results or from your presence, ideally both.

ideas.idea: A beauty editor is a business role: you must know your reader as deeply as the advertiser across the table and pitch ideas live that serve both.
ideas.detail: At Cosmo, beauty drove so much revenue that Leah reported almost equally to the publisher as to the editor-in-chief, sitting in live brainstorms with CMOs from P&G, Unilever and L'Oreal who wanted first-to-market ideas. She decided that mastering this would give her a long career.

ideas.idea: Work wives are essential to career survival: they are the only people who truly understand your context and let you vent instead of rage-quitting.
ideas.detail: Leah's core group (Holly, Meredith, Melissa, Jo) has moved companies together since Cosmo and speaks in shorthand. Cherie recalls her Zynga work wife Maya and their vent walks ending in three-minute hugs. Leah's therapist prescribes the walk and hug when she wants to hit the eject button, and notes that jumping ship rarely resolves the same frustrations.

ideas.idea: Women can lead with open gratitude and love, which makes direct feedback land better and creates a more collaborative team than the 'alpha' posture women once felt they had to adopt.
ideas.detail: Saying 'I love you so much, but there's one thing we need to sit on' gets a colleague to a middle ground far better than 'that's terrible, go change it.' Others on the team see and respect that leadership style, and it trickles down.

ideas.idea: 'Just say yes' as a life motto: saying yes creates the serendipitous moments that change your life, and saying no too often means you go nowhere.
ideas.detail: Leah met her husband at a Halloween party she almost skipped, and got her first job by putting a resume in a folder she had no business submitting. When her boss asked her to run the Entertainment group (People, EW, People en Espanol) after the Meredith acquisition, she first said no, slept on it, then said yes; it became the best decision of her career.

ideas.idea: When someone sees something in you that you do not see in yourself, trust it and at least try, asking 'what's the best that can happen?' instead of the worst.
ideas.detail: Leah says she would never have raised her hand for the entertainment role; her boss saw it for her. The hosts connect this to their own leap from tech into a podcast and physical product with Sisters Matcha.

ideas.idea: There is beauty in being naive: you can learn a whole new business on the job by trusting smart people, giving up control and researching what you do not understand.
ideas.detail: Moving from print to digital media felt like post-grad work; Leah emailed herself terms to Google later. Now she is launching an app knowing nothing about apps, relying on a room of smart people each doing what they do best.

ideas.idea: The best ideas arrive in the shower or in the ten minutes before sleep and after waking, and once you ship one thing you have a playbook you can reuse.
ideas.detail: Leah wonders how many people have genius ideas in those input-free moments and never act. Going through the process start to finish once gives you the confidence and template for the next thing.

ideas.idea: Workplace politics begins in middle management, where you are the jelly in the sandwich pleasing both your team and your boss, and must learn to lead with influence rather than force.
ideas.detail: Leah warns the boss you do dirty work for may disappear overnight; at Cosmo she lost her direct line to the chief content officer in 24 hours when leadership changed, and eventually left because she no longer believed in the direction.

ideas.idea: Once you have kids, a paycheck is not enough; you must feel respected, keep learning and see a path, and when the respect stops you have to go.
ideas.detail: Leaving her children for nine hours a day made fulfillment non-negotiable; she could have toughed out Cosmo another year or two with her thick skin but would not have been happy.

ideas.idea: Take the emotion out of feedback in the room: the CEO not liking your work is not him not liking you, so find the fixable core and fix it, then process the feelings outside with work wives, husband and therapist.
ideas.detail: After 25 years Leah still has to practice this. Her tactic is to box the energy and put it on a shelf, walk in stone-faced, take it in, walk out and go on a 'rage walk.' Having an outlet where all feelings are allowed is what makes it possible to show up unemotionally and execute.

ideas.idea: Therapy matters because workplace reactions to tone and energy trace back to your first 18 years, and naming the root gives you a toolkit and control.
ideas.detail: Leah traced a cortisol rush at work back to eighth-grade friends who dropped her. Knowing where the anxiety comes from means you know it will not last and what to do, instead of panicking about why you feel that way.

ideas.idea: Choose a partner who wants you to be as successful or more successful than they are; supportive partners leapfrog each other rather than compete.
ideas.detail: Leah dated people who could not handle her success before meeting Nick, five years younger and raised by a single mom to respect women; she called her aunt the day after meeting him to say she had found her husband. After 21 years they trade off travel and childcare as two executives.

ideas.idea: Do not assume that what came easily will always be easy; life will hand you mountains, like infertility, that you cannot make happen by force.
ideas.detail: Leah got pregnant immediately with her first child, then went through rounds of failed IVF and years of depression for the second before conceiving naturally. She frames female biology as sometimes competing with career growth, a blessing and burden with no universal formula, survivable with work wives, therapy and resilience.
